items.title: Celebrity chef Matty Matheson bringing Toronto restaurant to Mississauga
items.summary: A popular pizza restaurant run by one of the country’s best-known celebrity chefs is opening a brand new outpost in the 905 in the not-too-distant-future. Maker Pizza, a fast-growing Toronto-based pizza chain co-founded by chef Matty Matheson, will open its second suburban location–its first is in Thornhill–in Mississauga in a little over three weeks. According to Maker Pizza’s official website, the brand’s newest outpost will open its doors inside the up-and-coming Exchange District, a new residential development in Mississauga’s City Centre neighbourhood. Photo from Matheson’s official Facebook page The restaurant is slated to open, according to a countdown on the website, in 23 days. The new location was announced earlier this summer. The restaurant will take shape inside the Exchange Signature Residences, a 31-storey condo that’s close to Square One. While a menu for the Mississauga location has not yet been released, the restaurant is known for serving a variety of slices and pies, including a truffle shuffle, a Frank’s Best pizza with bechemel sauce, a Tropic Thunder pie with chilli-infused pineapple, a cheese pizza and more. The restaurant also offers chicken wings and garlic fingers.

items.title: Mississauga cements sister-city bond with Ternopil, Ukraine by renaming a park in its honour
items.summary: The two cities formally entered into a sister-city relationship earlier this year. Gulleden Park has been renamed Ternopil Park to honour Mississauga’s new sister-city partnership with the Ukrainian city. Mississauga’s Gulleden Park has been given a new name to honour the city’s new sister-city partnership with Ternopil, Ukraine. The renaming of the park, located at 3570 Havenwood Dr. in Ward 3, to Ternopil Park was approved at council’s July 29 meeting. The two cities formally entered into a sister-city relationship earlier this year, promising to strengthen ties between the two communities and create new opportunities for collaboration. According to the motion, the park was selected due to its proximity to St. Sofia Byzantine Catholic Elementary School — which offers a Ukrainian bilingual program — and its proximity to the neighbourhood where many residents of Ukrainian heritage live. “The renaming of Ternopil Park is a meaningful symbol of the friendship between Mississauga and Ternopil and of the strong ties we are building through our sister-city partnership,” stated Mississauga Mayor Carolyn Parrish in a news release. This is the second park in Mississauga named after a sister-city, joining Kariya Park, which opened in 1992 to mark the city’s sister-city relationship with Kariya, Japan, according to the motion.

items.title: African psychedelic linked to fatal healing ceremony, Mississauga man charged
items.summary: A Mississauga man is facing criminal charges after a Waterloo Region resident died following what police describe as a private healing ceremony involving ibogaine, a psychoactive substance that is not authorized for use in Canada. The Waterloo Regional Police Service says its General Investigations Unit launched a sudden death investigation on July 4 following the death of a man. Investigators allege the man had arranged to take part in a private ibogaine healing experience before his death. According to police, the deceased consumed ibogaine, a psychoactive alkaloid extracted from the root bark of a shrub native to Central West Africa. Health Canada has not approved ibogaine as a medical treatment, and it is not authorized for use in Canada. As part of the investigation, police raided a residence in Mississauga on July 30. Officers say they seized suspected ibogaine along with several other powders, liquids and capsules, which have been submitted to Health Canada for analysis. As a result of the investigation, 57-year-old Luis Da Silva has been charged with criminal negligence causing death and selling a prescription drug recklessly. Police have not released details about where the alleged healing ceremony took place or identified the deceased.

items.title: Toronto neighbourhood named after former Mississauga man
items.summary: A Toronto neighbourhood is named after a former Mississauga man who helped build one of the oldest log cabins in Ontario. As the City of Mississauga celebrates Leslie Log House’s 200th anniversary this weekend, it is interesting to note the name’s connection to Toronto’s Leslieville neighbourhood. Built in 1826, Leslie Log House is one of the oldest surviving log homes in Ontario and is a designated heritage property. The home is now located at 4415 Mississauga Rd. in Streetsville, but it was originally built just north of Derry Road in Meadowvale. In 1994, the house was moved to its current location. , his wife, Esther Beattie Leslie, and their children, built and lived in the home after they came to Upper Canada from Scotland. The log house was built on the southern half of a 200-acre property the family leased from King’s College. The family later purchased the land, and it remained in the family for 100 years. One of the Leslie sons, George Leslie, was the namesake for the east Toronto neighbourhood, Leslieville, according to Joanne Doucette’s book, Leslieville, published in 2016. The Leslie family sailed to Canada in 1825, landing in Quebec in mid-May of that year, Doucette said. ” John Leslie travelled alone first to the Meadowvale property in what was then Toronto Township, now Mississauga.

items.title: Why a dangerous invasive plant is being targeted with herbicide in Mississauga
items.summary: A plant that can cause painful skin burns is being targeted along Mississauga’s Etobicoke Creek Trail as the city works to control the spread of an invasive species. The City of Mississauga will begin a targeted herbicide application on Wednesday, Aug. 5, to treat wild parsnip, an invasive plant that can pose a health risk to people who come into contact with its sap. The treatment has raised the usual concerns that come with herbicide use in public spaces, but the city says the application will be highly targeted, with crews applying the product directly to the invasive plants while taking steps to limit impacts on surrounding vegetation. Mississauga Ward 3 Councillor Chris Fonseca alerted residents about the upcoming work, which will take place along the Etobicoke Creek Trail. , will apply VisionMax (glyphosate) using handheld and backpack sprayers, allowing workers to treat individual plants rather than broadly spraying the area. Wild parsnip is not native to Ontario and can quickly spread in sunny areas such as trails, roadsides, shorelines and forest clearings. Once established, dense patches can crowd out native plants and disrupt natural ecosystems. The plant also creates concerns for people using trails and parks. Wild parsnip contains sap that can cause a severe skin reaction when exposed to sunlight. Contact can lead to painful burns, and exposure to the eyes can cause serious injury, including blindness.

items.title: Loose Screens and Balcony Furniture Are Bigger Fall Risks Than Most Residents Realize, City Warns
items.summary: According to the City of Mississauga, falls from windows and balconies can cause serious injury or death, though the city says many of these incidents are preventable through simple precautions under its Balcony Basics awareness campaign. The city identifies common hazards as furniture placed too close to windows or balcony railings, windows left unsecured, and screens that were never designed to stop a fall in the first place. Young children face the highest risk, while older adults can be more vulnerable because of mobility or balance issues, the city says. Renters and highrise residents are encouraged to learn how to recognize these hazards themselves and report concerns early rather than waiting for something to go wrong. The responsibility doesn't stop with tenants. The city says property owners, landlords and building managers must also keep safety features in working order and respond quickly once a problem is flagged. Mississauga backs up the campaign with education, inspections and enforcement action aimed at preventing injuries before they happen.

items.title: Peel's Colour-Coded Health Inspection System Just Played Out at a Mississauga Restaurant
items.summary: According to INsauga, Peel Public Health records show that Charminar Indian Cuisine on Spectrum Way in Mississauga received a red card during an inspection on July 31, the most serious rating the agency issues. Inspectors found what the report describes as a significant risk of possible contamination or adulteration at the restaurant, serious enough to trigger an immediate closure. INsauga explains that a red card means an inspector found an actual health risk or danger, and under Peel's system that forces the establishment to close until the problem is fixed. Charminar has since been reinspected and given a green passing grade, allowing the restaurant to reopen. The outlet also notes the distinction with a yellow card, which signals a conditional pass where the establishment isn't fully meeting requirements under the Health Protection and Promotion Act but can keep operating while it fixes the issues. For Charminar's customers, the sequence shows how quickly a serious violation can shut a kitchen down, and how a passed reinspection gets it back open just as fast.
